endorsements.quote: AI can aid in detecting such cases, but the final clinical judgment must always remain with the physician.
Whenever feasible, patients and healthcare providers should be informed when AI systems are involved in diagnostic or therapeutic processes.

To this end, algorithmic models must be developed using inclusive and representative datasets, to mitigate the risk of perpetuating or exacerbating disparities based on gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, or geographic location.

Adequate training is essential to prevent—or at least mitigate—the risk of automation bias, defined as the uncritical or excessive reliance of clinicians on automated decisions and recommendations [ 56 ].
It is essential to promote the integration of AI education and training at all levels of medical education and continuing professional development [ 47 – 49 ].

In addition, we advocate for the implementation of formal procedures for reporting and investigating adverse events, near misses, and other safety-related incidents linked to the use of AI in healthcare settings.

The integration of AI into healthcare should follow a process of “continuous improvement”, incorporating real-world testing, feedback from end users, and rigorous scientific validation across diverse clinical settings.

Developers should be held accountable not only for violations of binding legal obligations, but also for systematically disregarding recognized industry standards and ethical guidelines during the design and development of AI systems, especially where such standards contribute to risk mitigation and safe deployment.
The sustainability and ecological impact of AI should be carefully assessed and mitigated across the entire lifecycle, from development through deployment.

unlisted_practices: Implement AI technologies only within certified, GDPR-compliant, healthcare-specific software platforms rather than general-purpose AI tools.
Adopt codes of conduct and certification frameworks in healthcare institutions to ensure legal and ethical compliance of AI use.
Establish robust data governance frameworks with strict access controls and traceability of data usage.
Host clinical data repositories within the national healthcare system infrastructure where feasible.
Adopt explainable AI tools that produce clear, interpretable outputs clinicians can understand.
Involve clinicians in AI design, development, and validation, and have developers collaborate with medical scientific societies.
Require AI solutions to undergo prospective, multi-center clinical trials in environments different from those of development.
Update regulatory frameworks to accommodate evolving AI systems and post-approval modifications.
Public institutions should invest in research to identify and mitigate discriminatory outcomes of AI.
Establish multidisciplinary collaborations among government, academia, nonprofits and industry to develop fair, unbiased AI algorithms.
Provide dedicated support personnel to help vulnerable and low-digital-literacy patients access AI-driven care.
Limit AI use to clinically justified, high-value applications and prioritize energy-efficient methods such as transfer learning.
Direct patient interaction with AI should never replace the clinician.
Incorporate data-centric AI education on data quality, bias, and completeness into clinician training.
Deployers must use AI systems according to manufacturer instructions and applicable use conditions.

screen.reason: This is a position paper / guideline from the Italian Society of Internal Medicine outlining recommendations and governance principles for AI integration in clinical practice.
